description: We’re a two-person team taking on the challenge of creating health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions. We’re interested in space exploration, software, and using data to support crew health. We’re looking for teammates with experience in coding, data analysis, AI/ML, data visualization, hardware or UX/human factors. If you’re curious about building practical tools for astronaut health.
summary:
Long-duration astronauts will have to assess their own health with limited real-time help from Earth. Most health dashboards show a number and leave the interpretation to the reader. Astronaut Health Twin compares an astronaut against their own baseline and their own history, then shows the result as an interactive 3D body.

An astronaut records a check-up: 22 metrics including heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood, stress, exercise and vision, plus symptoms with severity and mission context such as workload, spacewalks and radiation events. The app compares each value against their personal baseline, their previous check-up and their mission trend, then scores six body systems and automatically opens the 3D body at the region the evidence points to. Each region explains the relevant NASA hazard, the official NASA risk category, why it matters in microgravity, and cites a NASA or CSA source.

The app deliberately does not diagnose or recommend treatment. It separates measurement, comparison, mission context and guidance, and the guidance comes from an approved next-step ladder. A test-enforced tripwire fails the build if generated copy ever claims a diagnosis.

It runs fully offline: no accounts, no server, no paid API.
details:
LIVE APP: https://himesh-codrr.github.io/ (no login, no install)

WHAT IT DOES

Astronaut Health Twin is an offline-first web and mobile app that turns a routine health check-up into an understandable next action. Three ideas sit behind it:

1. PERSONAL HEALTH HISTORY. Every astronaut differs, so the app compares an astronaut with their own baseline and their own previous check-ups, never against a population average. A reading can be normal for one crew member and unusual for another.

2. A 3D BODY AS THE INTERFACE. Health data becomes a tappable, rotatable body instead of rows of numbers. Six systems are modelled: head & eyes, heart & blood vessels, muscles & bones, immune & digestive, mind & sleep, and a whole-body radiation layer. After a check-up the body automatically focuses on the system with the most evidence, and mesh colour is computed from that astronaut's own data.

3. MISSION-AWARE CONTEXT. A change only means something next to what the astronaut was experiencing. The app records workload, spacewalks, disrupted sleep schedules and radiation events, and surfaces them alongside the health change.

BENEFIT AND IMPACT. On a Mars transit, communication delay makes real-time guidance from Earth impossible, so the crew must interpret their own data. The app shortens that loop from "here is a number" to "here is what changed, why it may have changed, and what to do next" — and it does so in a form a tired crew member can read in seconds.

HOW IT WORKS

The comparison engine is deterministic and auditable. It computes the change from baseline (with a 5% floor so noise is not reported as change), the change since the previous check-up, a fitted least-squares trend requiring at least three points, and a robust outlier test using median and median absolute deviation. Regions are ranked with strongly diminishing returns, so a single alarming signal cannot be outvoted by a wide region reporting many mild ones. The 3D scene is a pure function of that ranking.

Tools used: Expo SDK 58 and React Native (one codebase for iOS, Android and web), TypeScript, three.js with expo-gl and react-three-fiber for the procedural 3D anatomy, AsyncStorage for local persistence, and Vitest for the 88-test suite.

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

We chose procedural geometry rather than a downloaded human model: there is no third-party asset licence to clear, and a stylised figure cannot be mistaken for a medical scan of the astronaut. Safety was a design constraint from the start, not a disclaimer bolted on. The app never says "you have", "diagnose", "prescribe" or "treatment plan" — a test fails the build if that language ever appears.

We deliberately did NOT train a deep-learning model. Astronaut medical datasets are small and privacy-protected; a model trained on them would be unvalidatable, and a patient-facing system that emits diagnoses needs clinical oversight a prototype cannot have. Instead every sentence the app generates can be traced back to a number and a source.

Three fictional astronauts ship with the app, each with a different trajectory, so reviewers can confirm the app generalises rather than being tuned to one story.

WHAT A REVIEWER CAN CHECK IN ONE MINUTE

Add an astronaut and set their own baselines, then reload the page — the profile is still there. Mark a follow-up step done with a note and the progress counter updates. Export the handover as JSON, text or PDF: the PDF is real, selectable text with sparkline charts, generated on-device through the OS print engine. The Privacy tab states the offline guarantee as inspectable facts (record counts, storage keys, stored size) rather than a slogan — and a test walks the whole source tree and fails the build if any network call is ever added.
